fetched_contents.text: Low pH preempts bloom development of a toxic haptophyte Introduction Harmful algal blooms (HABs) of Prymnesium parvum are global phenomena occurring in marine, estuarine and inland ecosystems (Moestrup, 1994, Edvardsen and Paasche, 1998, Lundholm and Moestrup, 2006). Prymnesium parvum, commonly called “golden algae” and the “Texas tide,” is a mixotrophic flagellated haptophyte known to produce toxins that may severely impact aquatic organisms (Brooks et al., 2010). There is some debate whether P. parvum is invasive to inland systems (Lutz-Carrillo et al., 2010), or whether it has been present for many years, only recently becoming an environmental issue due to anthropogenic influences and climatological changes that favor P. parvum growth (Roelke et al., 2012). Either way, salinization (Roelke et al., 2010a, Roelke et al., 2010b) and eutrophication (Hallegraeff, 1993, Roelke et al., 2007, Roelke et al., 2010b) have created conditions that allow for the proliferation of P. parvum blooms in inland waters. In particular, some Texas inland reservoirs have experienced devastating P. parvum blooms and conservative estimates suggest that over 30 million fish (Southard et al., 2010) have been killed since 1985 when blooms were first observed in the Pecos River (James and De La Cruz, 1989). Prymnesium parvum is now present in at least 5 major river basins and has affected over 33 reservoirs in Texas (Southard et al., 2010). A recent P. parvum bloom in Dunkard Creek, Pennsylvania/West Virginia in 2009 highlights the expansion of this organism even further northward (Brooks et al., 2011a). To date, P. parvum is present in at least 18 states in the United States (Roelke et al., 2011). Of the toxins produced by P. parvum, prymnesin-1 and prymnesin-2 were initially characterized (Igarashi et al., 1998, Igarashi et al., 1999) and thus have historically been held responsible for toxicity to aquatic organisms. However, toxicity may not solely result from exposure to prymnesins, but from other products such as fatty acids (Henrikson et al., 2010), fatty acid amides (Bertin et al., 2012a, Bertin et al., 2012b), or toxins yet to be characterized (Schug et al., 2010). Whereas the adaptive functions of these toxins remain unclear, the resultant fish kills, thought to be caused by the disruption of ion regulation in gills, are severe (Yariv and Hestrin, 1961, Ulitzur and Shilo, 1966, Edvardsen and Imai, 2006). Though less understood, the effects of these toxins on other organisms within aquatic ecosystems may have equally severe impacts (Brooks et al., 2010). In particular, P. parvum can affect zooplankton grazers by reducing fecundity (Larsen et al., 1998, Granéli and Johansson, 2003a, Roelke et al., 2007, Brooks et al., 2010) and altering predator–prey dynamics (Skovgaard and Hansen, 2003, Barreiro et al., 2005, Olli and Trunov, 2007). Furthermore, differential sensitivities among species to toxins produced by P. parvum can cause shifts in planktonic community structure (Fistarol et al., 2003, Brooks et al., 2010, Schwierzke et al., 2010), with longer term consequences yet unknown. A number of factors apparently influence the magnitude of toxins produced by P. parvum in inland waters, as evidenced by inconsistent correlation between population density of P. parvum and observed toxicity in laboratory and field studies (Baker et al., 2007, Baker et al., 2009, Grover et al., 2007, Brooks et al., 2010, Valenti et al., 2010a). Physical system conditions that influence P. parvum bloom dynamics include salinity, temperature, light, and river inflows (Parnas et al., 1962, Rahat and Jahn, 1965, Reich and Parnas, 1962, Baker et al., 2007, Baker et al., 2009, Roelke et al., 2010a, Roelke et al., 2011, James et al., 2011, Schwierzke-wade et al., 2011), while chemical conditions include inorganic nutrient concentrations (Granéli and Johansson, 2003a, Granéli and Johansson, 2003b, Grover et al., 2007, Johansson and Granéli, 1999, Roelke et al., 2007, Valenti et al., 2010a). The interplay among these processes leads to counter-intuitive observations. For example, optimum conditions for growth result in lowest toxicity to fish for the Texas strain of P. parvum (Baker et al., 2007, Baker et al., 2009), which differ markedly from late winter/early spring conditions of Texas impoundments (Roelke et al., 2011) when bloom associated fish kills typically occur (Southard et al., 2010). Another chemical variable shown to affect the magnitude of P. parvum associated toxicity in marine and inland waters is pH. Over 50 years ago, Shilo and colleagues (Shilo and Aschner, 1953, Ulitzur and Shilo, 1964) demonstrated that P. parvum was not ichthyotoxic at pH 7 and below, but became consistently more toxic to fish at higher pH levels in studies at salinities typical of marine/estuarine ecosystems. Similar relationships between pH and toxicity were recently extended to inland waters by our research group. Valenti et al. (2010a) identified that the potency of P. parvum toxins increased at higher pH by conducting bioassays with Pimephales promelas and Daphnia magna as model aquatic organisms. Such relationships were consistently observed in laboratory studies with monocultures of P. parvum at various levels of nutrient limitation and in field studies of samples collected during extensive fish kills attributed to P. parvum (Valenti et al., 2010a). Interactions between pH and P. parvum may represent an important determinant of site-specific blooms, because natural, anthropogenic and climatological factors influence pH dynamics in surface waters and thus the ambient toxicity of a wide range of organic and inorganic stressors (Valenti et al., 2011, Brooks et al., 2011b). (c) 2007 TPWD PWD RP T3200-1404 (1/07) PWD RP T3200-1404 (1/2007) Guidelines for Golden Alga Prymnesium parvum Management Options for Ponds and Small Reservoirs (Public Waters) in Texas The golden alga Prymnesium parvum is a toxic organism capable of causing extensive kills of aquatic animals. Rivers, ponds and reservoirs in north-central and west Texas have been susceptible to these toxic algal events (Figure 2). These guidelines were developed to provide information and describe management options presently available for controlling golden alga toxic events in ponds and small reservoirs in public waters. The information is provided to help cities, water utilities, river authorities, and others evaluate options for addressing toxic events. Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD) is not funded or staffed to treat algal problems. However, TPWD wants to provide information for entities that manage affected waters should they decide to address toxic algal events. Numerous groups are concerned and involved with decisions on possible management efforts for toxic golden alga events in Texas public waters. These groups include regulatory agencies such as the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ), U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA), and the Texas Department of Agriculture (TDA); water utilities and other water controlling authorities such as drinking water suppliers and river authorities; and water users such as irrigators, recreational users, and landowners. The TCEQ regulates water quality standards for the state including water quality and drinking water standards. The TDA and USEPA regulate the use of pesticides in the state including the use of algaecides in public waters. Water suppliers transport water for industry, agriculture, and public consumption. There are numerous users of public waters including recreational fishers and boaters, irrigators, industry, and water utilities. Additionally, TPWD serves an important role in guiding decisions regarding nuisance aquatic vegetation in public waters. All these stakeholders should be considered when making management decisions for toxic golden alga events. The natural concentrations of SO42- in aquatic systems show significant variability depending on the prevailing catchment geology and hydrology (Kleeberg, 2012). Since industrialisation began, the burning of fossil fuels has oxidised and released massive amounts of geologically bound sulfur into the atmosphere (Stoddard et al., 1999). Despite significant reductions in anthropogenically derived atmospheric sulphur (S) deposition across large parts of North America and Europe over the last decades, the current SO42- concentrations remain above natural background levels in surface and groundwaters and have even been increasing since the mid-20th century (Caraco et al., 1993; Zak et al., 2006; Kleeberg, 2012). The US inland water literature shows that harmful algal blooms are widespread and that cyanobacteria are the most common toxigenic algae in inland waters, while P. parvum is a major toxic alga with documented impacts in Texas and other states [N3-R2]. The Texas P. parvum management report emphasizes that blooms are most common in intermediate salinity and under moderate environmental stress, and that they have affected at least 15 U.S. states, including 29 reservoirs in Texas with large fish mortality and recreational losses [N4-F2]. This suggests that sulfate-related limnology is part of a broader regional picture of salinity, nutrient, and stress conditions.

On regional differences, the sulfate evidence points to variability across catchments and hydrology. The freshwater sulfate review notes that natural sulfate concentrations in aquatic systems vary widely depending on geology and hydrology, and that current concentrations remain above natural background levels in many surface and groundwater systems [N5-F3]. It also states that sulfate pollution is not limited to industrial or agricultural sources but results from a variety of human activities and that sulfate concentrations are persistent and increasing in many areas [N5-F3]. In inland waters, this matters because sulfate concentrations can differ across watersheds and land-use types, affecting nutrient availability, microbial processes, and overall water quality [N5-F3]. However, the evidence provided here does not give a detailed map of sulfate gradients across US inland waters, so any regional inference is provisional.

Regarding where P. parvum blooms are more likely under high sulfate conditions, the direct evidence is mixed and indirect. The N4 material says that P. parvum bloom formation is most common when cells are in intermediate salinity and under moderate environmental stress, and that ammonium sulfate is used to control blooms [N4-R2]. Land use, watershed inputs, and seasonality affect sulfate-bloom coupling through nutrient and salinity inputs. The N2 report notes that salinization and eutrophication have created conditions favoring P. parvum blooms in inland waters [N2-F1]. ## 3) Limitations, gaps, and uncertainties in the current evidence base

The branch reports show that many factors influence bloom magnitude, including salinity, temperature, light, river inflows, and inorganic nutrient concentrations [N2-F1]. They also note that observed toxicity can be inconsistent with population density, suggesting that nutrient limitation, environmental stress, and species-specific sensitivities matter [N2-F1]. The N4 material adds that bloom formation is most common in intermediate salinity and moderate environmental stress, and that management practices can alter water chemistry [N4-R4][N4-R2]. The sulfate review similarly points to pH, heavy metals, and nutrient mobility as confounding pathways [N5-F3]. These confounders mean that observed sulfate-bloom relationships may reflect indirect effects, not a direct causal link.

The available studies describe associations between sulfate-related conditions, salinity, pH, nutrients, and bloom occurrence, but they do not establish a direct sulfate-driven mechanism for P. parvum growth or toxin production [N2-F1][N4-R4][N5-F3]. The N2 report’s discussion of pH and toxicity shows that higher pH can increase toxin potency, but it also notes that optimal growth conditions do not always correspond to peak toxicity [N2-F1]. ## 4) Bottom line

Elevated sulfate concentrations in inland US waters likely affect P. parvum blooms indirectly, through nutrient cycling, microbial physiology, and interactions with pH and salinity [N5-F3][N1-R5][N2-F1]. However, the evidence does not support a simple conclusion that sulfate alone promotes or inhibits P. parvum growth; instead, sulfate appears to be part of a broader stress matrix that includes salinity, nutrients, pH, and seasonal conditions [N2-F1][N4-R4]. Regionally, sulfate concentrations interact with limnology, land use, watershed inputs, and seasonality to shape bloom distribution, but the evidence base is uneven and context-dependent [N3-R2][N4-F2][N5-F3].

Overall, the current evidence suggests that sulfate is a relevant but not dominant driver of P. parvum blooms. It is better understood as a modifier of bloom dynamics, rather than a primary cause [N2-F1][N4-R4][N5-F3]. For practical management and policy, this means that sulfate should be considered alongside salinity, nutrients, pH, and other environmental stressors, while remaining cautious about overinterpreting correlation as causation [N2-F1][N4-R4][N5-F3].
